newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Yachting - Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.
newsitem.headline: Australian Yachting - Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.

text.p: By Peter Campbell*
For the first time in Olympic history, an Australian-designed sailing boat, the Bethwaite 49er, will be one of the 10 yachting classes to be used at the Sydney 2000 Games.
The Events Committee of the International Sailing Federation (ISAF) early today recommended to that the 49er be the new Olympic high performance dinghy.
While the classes have to be ratified by the ISAF Council tomorrow, the inclusion of the 49er looks certain.

However, the Council may make some changes to the final line-up for Sydney 2000 with the Events Committee recommending dropping the ageless Star keelboat class to make way for the Bethwaite 49er after a long and emotive debate at its conference at Brighton, England.
Most pundits had predicted that the Finn single-handed dinghy would have been dropped while Australian delegates voted for discarding the 470 men s dinghy class.

The Events Committee has also recommended that four out of five Olympic sailing courses be sailed within Sydney Harbour, with only one course off the Heads, and that the yachting onshore site be at Rushcutters Bay.

Designed by innovative father and son team, FRANK and JULIAN BETHWAITE, the 49er is a skiff-style, open dinghy sailed by two persons on trapeze, with equal performance by men and women and light and heavy crews.
It was the outstanding dinghy at recent trials in Italy and England and the inclusion of a high performance dinghy for the Sydney Olympics was strongly promoted by ISAF President PAUL HENDERSON.

Henderson told the opening session of the ISAF conference at Brighton, England, that the federation must chose boats that would ensure that there would two million people sitting on the shore watching the sailing, with many millions more watching it on their TV screens across the world.
The Events Committee decision to recommend dropping the Star class keelboat from Olympic status comes as a surprise, ending the longest single run by any class.

The Star, a two-person keelboat in which Australians COLIN BEASHEL and DAVID GILES won the bronze medal at the Atlanta Games, has been an Olympic class since the 1930s, with the exception of the Montreal Games when it was replaced by the Tempest.
It means there will be only one keelboat class in Olympic yachting.
The Events Committee has recommended that the 10 Olympic classes for Sydney 2000 be:
-- Mistral Men sailboard
-- Mistral Women sailboard
-- Europe single-handed dinghy, women
-- Bethwaite 49er two-handed dinghy, open
-- Finn single-handed dinghy, men
-- Laser single-handed dinghy, open
-- Tornado two-handed multihull, open
-- 470 men, two-handed dinghy
-- 470 women, two-handed dinghy
-- Soling three-handed keelboat, open

The ISAF will vote tonight and feelings at Brighton are that while the 49er is certain of inclusion, moves may be made to change the other classes to still retain the Star at the expense of another class, possibly the 470 men or Finn single-handed dinghy.
YOUTH WORLDS FOR SYDNEY
Australia gained a major coup at the ISAF meetings when the Youth Committee earlier this week recommended that the ISAF World Youth Sailing Championships be held on Sydney Harbour in January 2000.
It will be the first international sporting event in Sydney in the Olympic year, with the Olympic Games set down for September.
The Yachting Association of NSW made a strong submission at the recent 1996 Youth Championships held in the USA and followed this with another submission at the ISAF meeting.

The championships will bring the world s outstanding teenage sailors from some 40 nations to Sydney, sailing in dinghy and sailboard classes, with the event based at Manly and sailed on the Harbour over the first week in January.
SYDNEY TO HOBART ENTRIES DOWN SLIGHTLY

Applications to enter the Telstra Sydney to Hobart closed last weekend but with 95 yachts being nominated by owners or charterers in all Australian States, the USA, Great Britain, Germany and New Zealand.
However, with some yacht nominations still in the mail the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia is confident the fleet will be just over the 100 mark when entries officially close at the end of November.

Last year the club received 106 entries and 98 yachts started. While there has been a boost in new boat launchings and an increased interest in offshore racing, the major decline is in entries from Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia where many owners have decided to contest the 25th annual Melbourne to Hobart West Coaster race.
Entries for the West Coaster, which starts from Port Phillip on December 27, are expected to be around the 60-boat mark, nearly double the recent fleets for that race.

Nevetheless, the quality of the Sydney to Hobart has been maintained at international standard with one of the best IMS fleets in the world competing, headed by Australia's winning team at the 1996 Kenwood Cup in Hawaii - SYD FISCHER'S Farr 50, Ragamuffin, GIORGIO GJERGJA'S Farr 47, Ausmaid, and BOB STEEL'S Nelson/Marek 43, Quest.
However, they will face strong competition from Beau Geste, a Farr-designed Corel 45 which was the IMS overall winner of the recent San Francisco Big Boat Series.

Beau Geste has been chartered by Sydney businessman RAY ROBERTS who is planning an America's Cup Challenge in 2000. Roberts has had great success in Australia and overseas races with his Iain Murray-designed BH41s and will be a strong competitor in this year's Sydney to Hobart.
Only one overseas maxi yacht has entered for the Sydney to Hobart - the Reichel/Pugh 80-footer Morning Glory, owned by German industrialist and co-founder of SAP computer systems, HASSO PLATTNER.
Sayonara, which Californian computer boss LARRY ELLISON, CEO of Oracle, sailed to a line honours win last year with RUPERT MURDOCH in the crew, is not coming down under this year.

Morning Glory was built in Sydney by JOHN MCCONAGHY, who has built our recent America's Cup challengers and is regarded as one of the best in the world in building yachts and masts from exotic composite materials such as kevlar and carbon fibre.
However, the yacht was never raced in Australian waters, going overseas in early 1995 to take line honours in record time in the Cape Town to Rio Race.
She is currently in New Zealand being fitted with a new mast for the Telstra Cup and Telstra Sydney to Hobart.

The race for line honours and the A$300,000 cheque which Telstra has put up for the first yacht to break Kialoa's 21-year-old race record of 2 days 14 hours 36 minutes 56 seconds, looks to be a duel between Morning Glory and Australia s fastest maxi, GEORGE SNOW's Brindabella, the Jutson 76 which last week took line honours in the Fujitsu Gosford to Lord Howe island race.
ELLE RACING BASED IN FREMANTLE

Amid some controversy, the Elle Racing campaign by an all-women crew to be the first Australian challenger for the Whitbread Round the World Race, is to be headquartered in Fremantle rather than skipper ADRIENNE CAHALAN and campaign head ELLE MCPHERSON'S home port of Sydney.
However, their new Whitbread 60 yacht is being built in Sydney, by JOHN MCCONAGHY.

The crew, currently training in a W60 from the previous round-the-world race, will fly the burgee of the Fremantle Sailing Club in their lead-up regattas and during the 1997-98 Whitbread, which includes stopovers in Fremantle and Sydney during the 27,000 nautical mile circumnavigation.
The reason they will be West Australian-based is the large financial incentive offered by the West Australian Government in contrast to no support out of New South Wales.

Western Australia has secured a tourism coup by securing the services of ELLE MCPHERSON who will appear in Brand WA tourism advertising campaigns promoting Western Australia through Australia and overseas.
The Tourism Commission is putting A$600,000 into the Elle Racing project and ELLE is also reported to be putting her fee into the campaign.
Meanwhile, negotiations are continuing between Cruising Yacht Club of Australia and Elle Racing to assist the crew in their Whitbread campaign.

The Club this week told Elle Racing they could not compete in the Telstra Sydney to Hobart in their Whitbread Race configuration as this includes water ballast which is not permitted under IMS (International Offshore System) rules.
It is likely that Elle Racing will compete in lead-up races and will then sail from Sydney to Hobart in a demonstration sail leaving just ahead of the official fleet.
We are anxious to help them in their Whitbread campaign as much as possible, CYCA Vice Commodore HUGO VAN KRETSCHMAR said this week.
* Peter Campbell is the editor of Offshore Yachting magazine.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800.
